analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide, with tradable allowances.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its energy subcommittee in fall 2003, it sat without action until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set hard national limits on four pollutants from fossil-fuel power plants — sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and, for the first time, carbon dioxide — enforced through a cap-and-trade allowance system. It gave plant owners free allowances and a promised 20-year period of regulatory stability, but in exchange stripped affected plants of some existing Clean Air Act obligations, including mercury toxic-emission standards and visibility protection rules. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it died without a markup or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, since the bill would force large cuts in the sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury those plants emit, and would cap their carbon dioxide for the first time. Owners of nuclear and renewable generating units also benefit, receiving tradable carbon allowances and access to a new-unit allowance reserve.

how_it_helps.text: Sets shrinking national tonnage limits for sulfur dioxide (from 4.5 million tons in 2009 to 2.25 million tons by 2016) and nitrogen oxides (1.7 million tons from 2013), pollutants tied to acid rain, smog, and respiratory illness.
Caps mercury emissions from coal plants at 24 tons in 2009-2012 and 10 tons from 2013, with per-unit limits, addressing a neurotoxin that accumulates in fish and reaches people through food.

Establishes the first statutory national cap on carbon dioxide from the electric generating sector, holding emissions at projected 2005 levels through 2012 and 2001 levels from 2013, enforced through a trading program with penalties.

Requires continuous emissions monitoring and quarterly reporting, with public release of emissions data and financial penalties ($5,000 per excess ton of NOx, $10,000 per pound of mercury, $100 per ton of CO2, inflation-adjusted).

analysis.who_pays: Owners of fossil-fuel power plants, especially coal-fired units, who would have had to buy allowances or install pollution controls, with some of those costs likely passed to electricity customers. Coal producers would face reduced demand as plants cut emissions or retired.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts affected power plants from mercury hazardous-air-pollutant standards under Clean Air Act Section 112 for eight years after enactment, trading away a toxic-emission control pathway in exchange for the tonnage cap.

It grants affected plants a temporary exemption from visibility-protection requirements lasting until 20 years after enactment, and rewires the new source review program so that beginning in 2009 it applies only to new units or changes that increase maximum hourly emission rates.
Allowances are given free to existing units based on past generation, which hands incumbent polluters a valuable asset, and the CO2 cap holds emissions at 2001 levels rather than cutting below them.

The lowest achievable emission rate standard is redefined to let cost considerations block required technology, and new plants locating in non-attainment areas after 2008 would not need emission offsets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, large public-health gains — mandatory cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and a first-ever CO2 cap — but bought them partly by exempting plants from other Clean Air Act protections and by grandfathering free allowances to existing polluters. It was a compromise: stricter than the administration's approach of the era but weaker than full enforcement of existing law. Honest supporters could call it a net win for downwind communities; honest critics could call it a shield for aging coal plants dressed as a cap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Charles Bass of New Hampshire introduced the Clean Air Planning Act of 2003 on September 16, 2003, joined by Representatives Davis of Florida, Cooper, and Bradley of New Hampshire.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On October 6, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, its last recorded action.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever taken on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of existing coal-fired power plants are better off, since no national carbon dioxide cap was imposed and no mandatory mercury, sulfur dioxide, or nitrogen oxide tonnage limits were added, leaving them under the existing regulatory regime. Coal producers also avoided pressure from a law that would have accelerated emission cuts and plant retirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired plant owners and coal producers

for.name: Rep. Charles F. Bass
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish national caps on four power plant pollutants, including carbon dioxide.

for.name: Reps. Jim Davis, Jim Cooper, and Jeb Bradley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a bipartisan if very small base of support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, leaving it to die in committee when the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 108th Congress, did not bring the bill to a committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four sponsors split evenly, two Republicans and two Democrats, but with no committee or floor votes the partisan shape of broader support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed real costs through mandatory tonnage caps, including a first-ever CO2 limit, but it also entrenches the industry: free allowances grandfathered to existing units, a promised 20-year regulatory freeze, and exemptions from mercury toxic-emission standards and visibility rules. The industry's preference for no bill at all ran against the public's interest in cleaner air.
Deep cuts in sulfur dioxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide from coal plants would reduce coal demand or force costly controls. The bill's death left coal demand and plant emissions unaffected.

The bill allocates carbon allowances to incremental nuclear generation and renewable energy units and sets aside reserves for new units, rewarding zero-carbon generation. This runs alongside the public interest in lower power-sector emissions.
